cold_first_call.definition: A cold call is the first call of a fresh process, measured as the warm-up call of the row (build_seconds of a row that is the first of its process). With the compiled caches kept, the process finds the Triton kernels and the torch extension of the HIP kernel on disk; with the caches cleared, the call compiles them, including the hipcc build of the HIP kernel.

session_note: every row is the median of 7 timed runs, with the minimum and the maximum, except as follows. The rows of the device (gpu, hybrid, tls-gpu, tls-gpu-binned, tls-gpu-pl, many, the block shuffles, the sizes of the GTLS paper's benchmark, the cold first calls, the split of the device time and the screening statistics) and the rows tls16 and tls16-exact of the table were measured in one session on one machine that started 2026-11-05T15:33:34Z UTC (load average 1.2) and ended at 2026-11-05T16:12:35Z UTC, with transitgpu at commit 9a94a40 plus the window search of a single period (f10787b). The release of 0.2.0 has further commits, which change no kernel of these rows (checks of arguments, a warning, a device guard, the build of the HIP source from the text read at import): the rows gpu and hybrid at 20,000 and 200,000 points, timed again on the last commit in two runs of 7 calls, were 0.98 to 1.04 times the medians of the session, torch 2.12.0+rocm7.2, triton-rocm 3.7.0, ROCm 7.2.4, Python 3.12.13, TLS 2.0.1, astropy 8.0.2 and wotan 1.10. Every part ran pinned to cores 0-15 on an otherwise idle machine with nothing else on the GPU (the session held the device exclusive and bench.py refused to start a row if another process held it); no part was stopped, resumed or run beside another job. The parts that time only the CPU rows were not run again, because no code of the package runs in them: the rows astropy, tls1 and tls1-exact, and the row tls16-many (64 light curves), are those of the session of 2026-10-26T04:56:28Z to 07:46:38Z UTC (astropy 8.0.1, the same TLS 2.0.1 and Python 3.12.13), and so is the row tls16-exact of the four runs of the GTLS input, which the session of 2026-11-05 did not run (the CPU rows of the parts were left out to keep the session to the device). Each such row carries measured_in_session. Beside them, a run of each of these CPU rows at 20,000 points on 2026-11-05 (one repeat, the same cores) gave, against the median of the session of 2026-10-26, astropy 1.010, tls1 1.011, tls16 0.990, tls1-exact 1.012, tls16-exact 0.984 and tls16-many 1.004 times the time, all within 1.6 percent. The device was 5.8 percent slower on 2026-11-05 than on 2026-10-26 for the row tls-gpu-pl: in an ABBA of that row and tls-gpu-binned at 20,000 points (5 repeats, v0.1.0, 9a94a40, 9a94a40, v0.1.0, each in its own environment, the same bench.py), tls-gpu-pl took 1.2400, 1.2397, 1.2424 and 1.2402 s (v0.1.0 measured 1.172 s on 2026-10-26), and tls-gpu-binned 1.1055, 1.1103, 1.1092 and 1.1045 s, so 0.45 percent more with 9a94a40. The first call of a fresh process with the compiled caches kept (the row tls-gpu) was timed once in the session and five times afterwards on the last commit, each in a fresh process: the build of the first call took 1.21 to 1.26 s (median 1.225 s) against the 1.246 s of the session and the 1.418 s of 2026-10-26, and its timed call at 20,000 points 2.91 to 3.15 s (median 2.921 s) against 2.874 s on 2026-10-26 (the single sample of the session, 4.313 s, was slow and is not cited). load_at_start in a row is the one-minute load average when the row starts, so it still contains the previous row's work and is not the load of an idle machine.
